conversion_pathway.process: Form-dependent folate processing and folate-cycle conversion supply 5-methyltetrahydrofolate; folic acid requires reduction.
conversion_pathway.limitations: This conversion pathway does not show that increasing folate intake increases tissue remethylation flux. Folic acid lowers blood homocysteine, which is a circulating marker. The primary source is a biochemical review, not a new human flux study. Reaction identity does not show that ordinary dietary intake controls tissue remethylation rate, and it does not assign clinical benefit. Phosphatidylethanolamine methylation is a later SAMe-consuming reaction, not part of this step.

food_evidence.limitations: Zeisel et al. (2003) Table 1, corrected by the erratum, reports 129 mg betaine per 100 g in raw beets. Canned beets in that table are 334 mg per 100 g. USDA Release 2 reports 130 mg per 100 g for the same raw NDB.

limitations: Supplemental betaine lowers plasma homocysteine in healthy adults, but that change does not measure tissue BHMT activity or show a clinical benefit. Human evidence is an eight-man depletion pilot, with the challenge response in four clinically depleted participants; tissue BHMT flux was not measured. Rat donor rescue and specific inhibition support the chain. This does not establish ordinary-diet limitation, response in every tissue or benefit above adequacy. Folate’s indirect constraint on BHMT remains unresolved.

nutrition_value_reviews.title: DHA observation: independent confirmation unresolved
nutrition_value_reviews.description: The archived USDA record reports DHA at 47 mg/100 g. Identity and unit conversion are verified, but independent confirmation of this amount in edible quinoa remains unresolved. The database observation is retained here, not replaced with zero or relabelled as ALA.
nutrition_value_reviews.decision: Temporarily withhold quinoa from DHA food lists and quantified rankings. The former 47 mg omega-3 total depended entirely on this held observation and is withheld too. Unqualified 18:3 remains separately unresolved. Reinstate only after review of supporting analytical identity and food basis.

conversion_pathway.process: Choline oxidation supplies betaine upstream of BHMT.
conversion_pathway.limitations: Choline oxidation can supply betaine, but increasing choline intake has not been shown to increase tissue BHMT flux. Human evidence is an eight-man depletion pilot, with the challenge response in four clinically depleted participants; tissue BHMT flux was not measured. Rat donor rescue and specific inhibition support the chain. This does not establish ordinary-diet limitation, response in every tissue or benefit above adequacy. Folate’s indirect constraint on BHMT remains unresolved. Choline oxidation can supply betaine, but increasing choline intake has not been shown to increase tissue BHMT flux. The enzyme evidence uses purified or recombinant human protein, not intact human metabolism. Loss of activity after removing zinc ligands does not show that dietary zinc usually limits the enzyme. The review statement that the pathway is independent of folate and vitamin B12 is not a new flux experiment. Quantitative claims in that review about choline deficiency and liver methionine were not re-checked in the primary animal papers. Purified, stable human choline dehydrogenase has been difficult to obtain, so some catalytic detail is inferred from related enzymes and from tissue activity rather than from a complete human kinetic characterisation. The reviews do not show that raising choline intake increases BHMT flux in people.

limitations: Cysteine is the substrate of the first assembly step. A formula that removed methionine and cysteine together slowed whole-blood synthesis, and that formula also removed methionine. conversion_pathway.process: Methionine can supply cysteine through upstream transsulfuration before glutathione assembly.
conversion_pathway.limitations: A formula that removed methionine and cysteine together slowed whole-blood synthesis, so that result does not isolate methionine. In the cysteine-free study, methionine intake stayed adequate and red-cell synthesis did not fall. This does not show that eating more methionine, once intake is adequate, raises glutathione synthesis. All three studies measured blood-cell, not neuronal, synthesis. The sulfur-amino-acid-free diet was an experimental amino-acid formula in seven young men for 10 days. The older-adult increase required combined supplementation and was not an isolated N-acetylcysteine or glycine test, not an ADHD trial, and not ordinary food. The cysteine-free arm used only four young men and two days of adaptation. Concentration did not track synthesis rate in the sulfur-amino-acid-free study.
